blocks.text: Richard was a little late in the morning, but I did not have to wait long for him. We walked into the park. The air was bright and wet with dew, and there was not a cloud in the sky. The birds sang beautifully. The drops of water shone on the ferns, the grass and the trees, and they were lovely to see. The woods seemed twenty times richer than they had been yesterday. In the quiet night they had looked so heavy and silent, as if they were asleep. But it seemed as if Nature had been more awake than usual that night. She had worked on every tiny detail of every wonderful leaf, to make that day glorious.
“This is a lovely place,” said Richard, looking round. “None of the noise and fighting of law-suits here!”
But there was other trouble.
“I tell you what, my dear girl,” said Richard, “when I get all my business settled, I think I shall come down here and rest.”
“Would it not be better to rest now?” I asked.
“Oh, as for resting now,” said Richard, “or doing anything very definite now, that's not easy. In short, it can't be done. At least, I can't do it.”
“Why not?” said I.

“You know why not, Esther. Imagine you were living in an unfinished house. The roof might be put on or taken off. The whole house might be pulled down or built up, from top to bottom—tomorrow, the next day, next week, next month, next year. You would find it hard to rest or settle. So do I. Now? There is no ‘now’ for us suitors, who are waiting on the court.”

When I saw that dark look from last night on his face again, I could almost have believed in the pull that my poor little wandering friend had talked about so much. It was terrible to think of, but his look also had a touch of that unfortunate man who had died.
“My dear Richard,” said I, “this is a bad beginning of our conversation.”
“I knew you would tell me so, Dame Durden.”
“And not only me, dear Richard. I was not the one who once warned you never to build a hope or expectation on the family curse.”

“There you go back to John Jarndyce!” said Richard impatiently. “Well! We must come to him sooner or later, because he is the main part of what I have to say. So we may as well do it now. My dear Esther, how can you be so blind? Don't you see that he has an interest in the case? It may suit him very well if I know nothing about the suit and care nothing about it. But it may not suit me quite so well.”

“O Richard,” I protested, “is it possible? You have seen him and heard him. You have lived under his roof and known him. And can you still speak such unworthy suspicions, even to me, in this lonely place where no one can hear us?”
His face went deeply red, as if his naturally generous nature felt a sharp sting of blame. He was silent for a little while. Then he replied in a quiet voice:
“Esther, I am sure you know that I am not a mean fellow. And I know, at least to some degree, that suspicion and distrust are poor qualities in a man of my age.”
“I know it very well,” said I. “I am not more sure of anything.”

“That's a dear girl!” Richard replied, “and just like you, because it gives me comfort. I needed to get some small piece of comfort out of all this business. It is a bad business even at the best, and I don't need to tell you that.”

“I know perfectly well,” said I. “I know just as well, Richard—what shall I say?—as well as you do, that such wrong ideas about people are not natural to you. And I know, as well as you know, what changes your nature so much.”

“Come, sister, come,” said Richard, a little more cheerfully. “You will be fair with me, at least. If I have the bad luck to be under that influence, so is he. If it has twisted me a little, it may have twisted him a little too. I don't say that he is not an honourable man, apart from all this confusion and uncertainty. I am sure he is. But it spoils everybody. You know it spoils everybody. You have heard him say so fifty times. Then why should he escape?”
